Summary: Covenant is the framework of Israel's relationship with God: a binding bond, sealed by promises, signs, and obligations, running from Noah and Abraham through Sinai to David.
JewishBackground: In Jewish thought God relates to his people not by vague goodwill but by covenant (berit): a sworn, binding relationship with both promise and responsibility. The covenant with Abraham promised descendants and land, sealed by circumcision; the covenant at Sinai bound the redeemed people to Torah, sealed with sacrifice; the covenant with David promised an enduring throne. Each covenant has a sign, a story, and a demand: God keeps his word, and Israel is called to keep hers.
PointsToChrist: The New Testament presents Jesus as the mediator of a new covenant, promised in Jeremiah 31 and sealed by his blood at the Last Supper: 'This cup is the new testament in my blood' (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews sets out how the new covenant fulfils what Sinai foreshadowed. TRADITIONAL reading: Messianic readers also see the Abrahamic promise — 'in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed' — as reaching its full scope in the inclusion of the Gentiles through Christ.
Scripture: Genesis 15:17-21; Genesis 17:9-14; Exodus 19:5-6; Exodus 24:3-8; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6-13
